Forests in Small Spaces

A pocket forest—a dense planting of native trees and shrubs on a small urban site—create[1] layers of vegetation where there may once have been lawn or bare ground. Young plants are placed close together, encouraging them to grow upward as they compete for light. Fallen leaves are usually left beneath them, where the material protects soil and gradually decomposes.

Although the name includes the word forest, a pocket forest is not simply a full-size woodland squeezed into a tiny lot, but instead it is[2] a planned community of locally suited plants. Designers may induct[3] tall canopy species, shorter understory trees, and shrubs that flower at different times. Some projects begin with schoolyards, while others occupy narrow strips beside offices or apartment buildings.[4]

Once the planting plan is established, community participation becomes especially visible.[5] Volunteers spread mulch, monitor moisture, and replace seedlings that fail during the first seasons. As the plants become established, the site requires less frequent care and offers shade, habitat, and a place to observe seasonal change.
